PbWCFNIzho8.title: Consistency in Good Deeds
PbWCFNIzho8.one_line: A reminder on keeping up good habits after Ramadan, based on the Prophet's advice not to abandon night prayer once started.
PbWCFNIzho8.summary: The speaker builds on the Prophet's advice to Abdullah ibn Amr not to be like a man who used to pray at night and then stopped. The criticism was not for never praying but for stopping. Starting a good deed is beautiful, but what pleases Allah more is sticking with it, such as continuing night prayer, Quran reading and dua after Ramadan. He pairs this with the hadith that the most beloved deeds to Allah are the consistent ones even if small. He warns against Shaytan's suggestion to skip just today, since a day becomes weeks and the habit is lost. When tired or short on time, reduce the amount but never stop completely, and make it up the next day.

outline.heading: Do not be like the one who stopped night prayer
outline.gist: The Prophet criticized stopping a good deed, not never starting it.

outline.heading: Sticking to habits after Ramadan
outline.gist: The most beloved deeds are consistent, even if small.

outline.heading: Reduce but never stop
outline.gist: Resist 'skip it today'; do a smaller portion rather than lose the habit.

MikgUhW4S7Q.speaker: guest
MikgUhW4S7Q.speaker_note: untitled khaterah during the sheikh's three-week trip; younger speaker who mentions seeing things in Egypt and refers to his own earlier khaterahs
MikgUhW4S7Q.title: No True Life but the Life of the Hereafter: Four Keys to Zuhd
MikgUhW4S7Q.one_line: Zuhd as an inner detachment from the dunya, explained through Hatim al-Asamm's four reasons for his detachment.
MikgUhW4S7Q.summary: Starting from the hadith of Anas that there is no true life except the life of the hereafter, the speaker defines zuhd as an inner state of the heart: detaching from worldly pleasures and prioritizing preparation for the hereafter. He separates it from poverty, noting that the rich can be detached and the poor deeply attached, as he saw among people in Egypt focused on brands despite hardship. He then offers the explanation of an early scholar, Hatim al-Asamm, who named four things behind his detachment. First, his provision was decreed and no one else would take it, which settles the heart; chasing rizq as an end ties us to the world, made worse by hedonic adaptation. Second, no one would perform his duties for him, so he busied himself with them, without dismissing shared work. Third, Allah sees him, so he felt shame to be seen in disobedience. Fourth, death awaits, so he prepared to meet his Lord; remembering the destroyer of pleasures is the most sobering of the four.

outline.heading: The hadith: no life but the life of the hereafter
outline.gist: The Prophet repeated this phrase in several contexts; its lesson is zuhd.

outline.heading: What zuhd is and is not
outline.gist: An inner detachment of the heart, not poverty; the poor can be attached and the rich detached.

outline.heading: Hatim's first key: provision is decreed
outline.gist: Knowing rizq will reach you settles the heart; chasing it as an end feeds hedonic adaptation.

outline.heading: Hatim's second key: your deeds are yours alone
outline.gist: No one will act on your behalf, and each answers to Allah individually.

outline.heading: Hatim's third key: Allah is watching
outline.gist: Shame before Allah; a pleasure bought with His displeasure is no pleasure.

outline.heading: Hatim's fourth key: death awaits
outline.gist: Remembering death, the destroyer of pleasures, prepares the heart to meet Allah.

Z9bjJ1P4CmU.title: Obligations Before Extras
Z9bjJ1P4CmU.one_line: Using the hadith of the man who would add nothing to the obligations, the speaker urges perfecting the fard and acting on knowledge.
Z9bjJ1P4CmU.summary: The speaker narrates the hadith in Bukhari of the man who asked about Islam and was told of the five prayers, Ramadan and zakat, each time learning there was nothing more required unless voluntary. He swore he would neither add nor reduce, and the Prophet said he would succeed if truthful. The lesson is that people often chase extras while neglecting obligations: praying extra but missing Fajr, posting reminders while neglecting parents, memorizing Quran without lowering the gaze. Obligations are the foundation, voluntary acts beautify the house, and those steady on the obligations should then seek what brings them closer. He contrasts our abundant access to knowledge with the companions' immediate action, citing Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, whose death shook the Throne after only six years as a Muslim.

8y7hH1bcBaM.title: The Prudent and the Incapable
8y7hH1bcBaM.one_line: The hadith of the prudent who holds himself accountable and works for the hereafter, versus the incapable who follows desire and presumes on Allah's mercy.
8y7hH1bcBaM.summary: Continuing a series on detachment from this world, the speaker explains the hadith contrasting the prudent person, who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, with the incapable person, who follows his desires and simply hopes Allah will forgive. Prompted by a physician's question about what distinguishes a successful Muslim, he illustrates prudence with missing a cheap flight by waiting. He warns against a 'you only live once' mindset and the claim that Allah knows my heart so I need not pray, and urges accountability even for lost opportunities.

CkOb9MbDYUM.title: Knowledge That Benefits
CkOb9MbDYUM.one_line: Knowledge in Islam is for action: acting on what you know is the gateway to more knowledge.
CkOb9MbDYUM.summary: Starting from the Prophet's prayer for refuge from knowledge that does not benefit, the speaker argues that seeking knowledge as an end in itself misunderstands why Islam stresses it. He draws on al-Hasan al-Basri's two kinds of knowledge, of the heart and of the tongue, Ibn Mas'ud's saying that knowledge is what produces awe of Allah, the hadith on knowledge that keeps benefiting after death, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's remark that failing to act on what they knew kept them from more. Teaching and applying deepen understanding, and acting on what one has eases the anxiety of feeling behind.

outline.gist: The Prophet sought refuge from useless knowledge, an unhumbled heart, an insatiable self and an unanswered prayer.

outline.gist: Ibn Mas'ud: knowledge is not many narrations but what brings fear of Allah.

outline.heading: Knowledge that benefits after death
outline.gist: Deeds end at death except beneficial knowledge that others learn and act on.

outline.heading: Passing it on is the prophets' legacy
outline.gist: Teaching and applying, not only attending classes, is the way to more knowledge.

outline.heading: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: action unlocks knowledge
outline.gist: Their shortfall in acting on what they knew kept them from further knowledge.

outline.heading: Teaching clarifies, and easing the fear of missing out
outline.gist: Concepts click when taught; acting on what you have relieves the anxiety of chasing more.

13:19.ar: ۞أَفَمَن يَعۡلَمُ أَنَّمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيۡكَ مِن رَّبِّكَ ٱلۡحَقُّ كَمَنۡ هُوَ أَعۡمَىٰٓۚ إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ أُوْلُواْ ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰبِ
13:19.en: Is he who knoweth that what is revealed unto thee from thy Lord is the truth like him who is blind? But only men of understanding heed

13:20.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يُوفُونَ بِعَهۡدِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَا يَنقُضُونَ ٱلۡمِيثَٰقَ
13:20.en: Such as keep the pact of Allah, and break not the covenant

13:21.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ يَصِلُونَ مَآ أَمَرَ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦٓ أَن يُوصَلَ وَيَخۡشَوۡنَ رَبَّهُمۡ وَيَخَافُونَ سُوٓءَ ٱلۡحِسَابِ
13:21.en: Such as unite that which Allah hath commandeth should be joined, and fear their Lord, and dread a woeful reckoning

13:22.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ صَبَرُواْ ٱبۡتِغَآءَ وَجۡهِ رَبِّهِمۡ وَأَقَامُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأَنفَقُواْ مِمَّا رَزَقۡنَٰهُمۡ سِرࣰّ ا وَعَلَانِيَةࣰ وَيَدۡرَءُونَ بِٱلۡحَسَنَةِ ٱلسَّيِّئَةَ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمۡ عُقۡبَى ٱلدَّارِ
13:22.en: Such as persevere in seeking their Lord's Countenance and are regular in prayer and spend of that which We bestow upon them secretly and openly, and overcome evil with good. Theirs will be the sequel of the (heavenly) Home

13:23.ar: جَنَّٰتُ عَدۡنࣲ يَدۡخُلُونَهَا وَمَن صَلَحَ مِنۡ ءَابَآئِهِمۡ وَأَزۡوَٰجِهِمۡ وَذُرِّيَّٰتِهِمۡۖ وَٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَدۡخُلُونَ عَلَيۡهِم مِّن كُلِّ بَابࣲ‏
13:23.en: Gardens of Eden which they enter, along with all who do right of their fathers and their helpmeets and their seed. The angels enter unto them from every gate

13:24.ar: سَلَٰمٌ عَلَيۡكُم بِمَا صَبَرۡتُمۡۚ فَنِعۡمَ عُقۡبَى ٱلدَّارِ
13:24.en: (Saying): Peace be unto you because ye persevered. Ah, passing sweet will be the sequel of the (heavenly) Home

8:2.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ ٱللَّهُ وَجِلَتۡ قُلُوبُهُمۡ وَإِذَا تُلِيَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتُهُۥ زَادَتۡهُمۡ إِيمَٰنࣰ ا وَعَلَىٰ رَبِّهِمۡ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ

13:25.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ يَنقُضُونَ عَهۡدَ ٱللَّهِ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مِيثَٰقِهِۦ وَيَقۡطَعُونَ مَآ أَمَرَ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦٓ أَن يُوصَلَ وَيُفۡسِدُونَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمُ ٱللَّعۡنَةُ وَلَهُمۡ سُوٓءُ ٱلدَّارِ

jyEKNBF-FwA.title: AI vs SI: Artificial and Spiritual Intelligence
jyEKNBF-FwA.one_line: Against reliance on artificial intelligence, the khatib describes spiritual intelligence through the traits of 'those of understanding' in Surah Ar-Ra'd.
jyEKNBF-FwA.summary: The khatib opens by noting how quickly people now depend on AI for answers that sound logical even when they cannot judge them, citing research forecasts about where AI will be by the 2040s. He contrasts this with spiritual intelligence, which the Quran attributes to ulu al-albab, those of understanding. Reading Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:19-24, he walks through their traits: fulfilling Allah's covenant, joining what Allah ordered joined, fearing their Lord and a bad reckoning, patience seeking Allah's face, establishing rather than merely performing prayer, spending secretly and openly, and repelling evil with good, with the reward of gardens and the angels' greeting. He supports the fear of Allah with Al-Anfal 8:2. In the second khutbah he reads 13:25 on those who break the covenant and cut ties, pointing to how easily marriages are broken in the community, and warns with An-Nisa 4:108 that people hide from others but not from Allah. He closes by urging support for the youth and the community's wellness work.

y18fBghNbRI.speaker: guest
y18fBghNbRI.speaker_note: untitled khaterah during the sheikh's three-week trip to Syria; different voice, reads the narration in Arabic then reflects briefly
y18fBghNbRI.title: Islam as a Badge of Honour: al-Harith al-Ghatafani at the Trench
y18fBghNbRI.one_line: The Ansar refuse to buy off Ghatafan with Madinah's dates at the Trench; is Islam a badge of honour or a target we hide?
y18fBghNbRI.summary: The speaker reads a narration from Abu Hurayrah: during the Battle of the Confederates, al-Harith al-Ghatafani came to the Prophet asking for half of Madinah's date harvest in return for withdrawing his tribe. The Prophet consulted the Sa'ds, leaders of the Ansar, who asked whether this was revelation, to be obeyed, or his own opinion. When he said it was a measure to protect them, they replied that they had never given such humiliation even before Islam, so they would not now that Allah had honoured them with it. He stresses that this happened at a moment of real fear, when hearts were in throats, yet they would not appear weak while carrying Islam, even when a strategic case could be made. He links it to Khubayb, who kept his two rak'ahs before execution short so no one would think he feared death. He then turns the question on himself and the audience in the West: do we treat Islam as a target to hide or a badge to wear, saying 'lunch' instead of 'prayer', or using questions about our prayer as an opening to speak about Islam.

outline.gist: At the darkest point of the siege they still refused to appear weak while carrying Islam.

outline.gist: He kept his prayer short before execution so his captors would not think he feared death.

I9gq-TGEXD0.title: Be in This World as a Stranger or a Traveller
I9gq-TGEXD0.one_line: A short reflection on the hadith of Ibn Umar, 'be in this world as a stranger or a traveller', against procrastination.
I9gq-TGEXD0.summary: The speaker takes the hadith in which the Prophet held Ibn Umar by the shoulder and told him to live in this world like a stranger or a wayfarer, along with Ibn Umar's own advice not to wait for evening once morning comes. He notes the advice was given to a young man who would assume he had decades ahead, and argues that everyone, not only Muslims, loves the comfort of 'later': later we will pray, give, serve the community. The hadith reverses this by asking us to treat each day and night as possibly the last, as with the advice to pray each prayer as a farewell prayer, which changes its quality. He then explains the two images. A stranger abroad goes for a benefit and returns home, as we are here to collect good deeds and return to the hereafter. A traveller in transit does not decorate or settle in the airport but passes through it. So worldly gain is welcome if it comes, but what matters is taking from this world what benefits the next.

e8UCYSsPiY4.title: Looksmaxing and the Best of Forms
e8UCYSsPiY4.one_line: A khutbah on beauty obsession, cosmetic extremes and social media, answered with the Quran's view of human form and the prophetic mirror dua.
e8UCYSsPiY4.summary: The speaker addresses a world saturated with images that change how we see ourselves, prompted by overhearing a young Muslim talk about looksmaxing. He describes extremes among young men and women, from bone breaking and unregulated supplements to filters and surgery, and notes that some Muslim-majority countries lead cosmetic surgery rates. Against this he sets the Quran: humans created in the best of forms, and diversity of colours and tongues as signs of Allah, not defects to fix. Social media amplifies faces and wealth, the two things Allah does not look at, pulling attention from hearts and deeds. He turns the mirror moment into the dua asking Allah to beautify character as He beautified form. In the second khutbah he names Shaytan's stated aim to alter Allah's creation, the power of what enters the eyes and the command to lower the gaze, and the Prophet's playful embrace of Zahir, telling him he is precious to Allah. He closes with looking to those who have less.

EFbGoi5WUJI.one_line: A reminder not to wait for perfect conditions before spiritually preparing to meet Allah, even during busy phases of life.
EFbGoi5WUJI.summary: Continuing a series on detaching from worldly ties to prepare spiritually, the speaker admits his own habit of postponing spiritual goals until school ends or until marriage. Drawing on a hadith and a commentary from a book of wisdom aphorisms, he argues that waiting for the perfect time is itself an obstacle: Allah placed you in your current busy phase and expects observance of Him within it. The remedy is not abandoning work but small, consistent acts woven through the day, which is why the five prayers interrupt the working day to remind us that Allah is greater than what we chase. He ends by urging himself and the audience to stop making excuses and keep turning to their Creator in busy seasons.

zrPNsWfzLnI.one_line: A reminder on the Prophet's advice to Muadh to ask after every prayer for help in remembrance, gratitude and excellent worship.
zrPNsWfzLnI.summary: The speaker narrates, with its chain passed on with love, the hadith in which the Prophet told Muadh ibn Jabal that he loved him and advised him never to leave, after every prayer, the dua asking Allah for help in remembering Him, thanking Him and worshipping Him well. The first lesson is to express love for the sake of Allah aloud rather than assume others know it. The second is that we need Allah's help even to worship Him. He then takes the three parts: remembrance; gratitude for blessings seen and unseen in health, family and faith, including being able to pray that night; and excellent worship, explained through ihsan, worshipping Allah as if you see Him. He ends with how each narrator passed the advice on.

SWygCBUAmCg.title: The Prophet's Dhikr When Returning From Travel
SWygCBUAmCg.one_line: The Prophet's words on coming home from Hajj, Umrah or battle, and the lesson that what matters is the state of heart you return in.
SWygCBUAmCg.summary: The talk explains the narration of Ibn Umar describing what the Prophet said whenever he came home from Hajj, Umrah or a military expedition: three takbirs, the declaration of Allah's oneness and sovereignty, then the words returning, repenting, worshipping, prostrating and praising our Lord, and that Allah fulfilled His promise, aided His servant and defeated the confederates alone. The speaker's lesson is that what counts is not the journey but the state one is in: if you are in submission, repentance, worship and praise of Allah, you are well, and if not, nothing else matters.

full.isnad_ar: حدثنا عبد الله بن يوسف، أخبرنا مالك، عن نافع، عن عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنهما
full.isnad_en: 'Abdullah ibn Yusuf from Malik from Nafi' from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar
full.ar_block: يروي الإمام البخاري في صحيحه، بسند صحيح، عن عبد الله بن عمر رضي الله عنهما: «أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم كَانَ إِذَا قَفَلَ مِنْ غَزْوٍ أَوْ حَجٍّ أَوْ عُمْرَةٍ يُكَبِّرُ عَلَى كُلِّ شَرَفٍ مِنَ الأَرْضِ ثَلاَثَ تَكْبِيرَاتٍ، ثُمَّ يَقُولُ: لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لاَ شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ الْمُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ، آيِبُونَ تَائِبُونَ عَابِدُونَ سَاجِدُونَ لِرَبِّنَا حَامِدُونَ، صَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ، وَنَصَرَ عَبْدَهُ، وَهَزَمَ الأَحْزَابَ وَحْدَهُ»
full.en_block: Imam al-Bukhari narrates in his Sahih, with a sahih chain, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both): "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) returned from a military expedition, Hajj or 'Umrah, he would say takbir three times on every rise of ground, then say: There is no god but Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion and His is the praise, and He has power over all things. Returning, repenting, worshipping, prostrating, praising our Lord. Allah has fulfilled His promise, aided His servant, and defeated the confederates alone."
full.note: Bukhari repeats it in several places (Jihad, Maghazi, Da'awat) through Nafi' and Salim.

takeaways: Learn and say the prophetic dhikr when coming home from travel.
Return from every journey in a state of repentance and praise.
Attribute any success to Allah alone.

esGMjPBntLA.title: Leaving What Does Not Concern You
esGMjPBntLA.one_line: A short reminder on the hadith that part of a person's good Islam is leaving what does not concern him.
esGMjPBntLA.summary: The speaker explains the hadith that leaving what does not concern you is part of the excellence of a person's Islam. He notes that the wording implies an active choice: you will be invited into idle talk, curiosity and pointless activity, and you must step away. He sorts what does not concern you into layers: the forbidden, the doubtful grey areas, the disliked, and the merely useless that brings no benefit in this life or the next. Since life passes quickly, he urges filtering out all of these and spending time and energy only on what benefits oneself, others and the community. He closes with a narration of a tribal leader who asked what to command his people, and was told to spread peace and speak only about what concerns them.

_9g07fZSeF4.title: Tasting the Sweetness of Faith
_9g07fZSeF4.one_line: A reminder on the hadith that one tastes faith who is pleased with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion and Muhammad as Prophet.
_9g07fZSeF4.summary: The speaker opens with the hadith of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib in Tirmidhi that whoever is content with Allah as Lord, Islam as religion and Muhammad as Prophet has tasted faith. He tells of a revert friend who, before Islam, had no direction or system for decisions, and found that after accepting Islam his decision-making became simple. Contentment with Islam means accepting its guidance when choosing. He points to the companions at the Battle of al-Ahzab, who asked the Prophet whether a decision was a command from Allah, ready to submit if it was. Those born into Islam often take this framework for granted when marrying or seeking work, and he urges reflecting on it so the sweetness of faith becomes a constant feeling.

3ZP0j6ZMPxc.title: When the Limbs Testify
3ZP0j6ZMPxc.one_line: A reminder from Surah Ya-Sin that our mouths will be sealed and limbs will testify, with a warning about careless words.
3ZP0j6ZMPxc.summary: The speaker opens with the verse of Surah Ya-Sin in which mouths are sealed on the Day of Judgment while hands speak and feet testify. In this life we are used to explaining and defending ourselves, but on that day no excuse or argument is possible and every limb bears witness, so the body we use is not truly ours. He then cites the agreed-upon hadith that a servant may say a word displeasing to Allah without a thought and fall into Hellfire because of it. Words said in anger, careless jokes or repeated gossip can carry heavy consequences. Yet the same tongue can be a source of great reward when it comforts, speaks the truth, encourages good and remembers Allah.
